newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazilian president gambles all on re-election bid. [CORRECTED 01:00 GMT 29/1]
newsitem.headline: Brazilian president gambles all on re-election bid. [CORRECTED 01:00 GMT 29/1]

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso on Tuesday prepared to gamble his political capital on a bid to amend Brazil's constitution to allow his re-election.

Congress officials said a bill allowing incumbent presidents, governors and mayors to seek a second consecutive term would be presented to the Chamber of Deputies in the afternoon and might be voted on in a late-night session.
"I am always optimistic when it comes to Brazil," Cardoso told reporters as he left his residence. "As far as specific subjects are concerned, we shall just have to wait and see."

Brazil banned the re-election of presidents when it became a republic in 1889 after the monarchy was abolished. But Cardoso argues that the economic reforms he launched as finance minister in 1994 need political continuity to prosper.

Analysts say the 30-month economic reform programme that has brought inflation under control will be strengthened if Cardoso gets his way and wins another four-year (corrects from "six-year") term in office, following the example of other Latin American presidents such as Argentina's Carlos Menem and Peru's Alberto Fujimori.

If his bid to amend the constitution is defeated, he will serve his two remaining years as a lameduck president. And his re-election project has stumbled into a minefield of opposition and vested interests.

A rebellious faction of the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB), which backs Cardoso, persuaded lawmakers to put off a vote on the re-election bill until the presidents of the lower and upper houses are chosen in February.

But a frantic government campaign to win over dithering congressmen and senators bore fruit over the weekend. Newspapers reported the government had mustered between 327 and 340 votes in favour of re-election in the lower house, more than the 308 needed to pass a constitutional amendment.
The bill must be passed twice in both the lower and upper houses, each time by a 60 percent majority.
The government continued to focus its efforts on Tuesday on making sure wayward politicians turned up in Brasilia, even hiring private jets to fly in sick deputies.
"Even corpses are being resuscitated," PMDB congressman Aloysio Nunes Ferreira told the Estado de Sao Paulo newspaper.
Carlos Alberto of the rightist Liberal Front Party (PFL), a backbone of Cardoso's fragile multiparty coalition, left a hospital where he has been treated for bone marrow cancer.
"We have to vote for re-election to bring Brazil into the First World," he told the Correio Braziliense daily.
